## The claim

In 2014 the original authors (OAs) emailed 1,017 public housing authorities in the United States, asking how to apply for public housing. Each email was signed with one of six names, meant to indicate a white, a Black or a Hispanic sender, and the name that each authority received was assigned at random. The OAs then recorded whether the authority replied, how quickly, and in what tone. One claim from their paper is our target:

> "Hispanic housing applicants were ... less likely to be greeted by name than were ... white counterparts" (Einstein and Glick 2017: 100)

This is a sentence of their abstract as the SCORE programme selected it for the Multi100 project, which gave it to five analysts to test. The published estimate is −20.0 percentage points (95% CI −30.5 to −10.0): the change in the predicted probability of a greeting by name from a white to a Hispanic name, from a logistic regression with covariates.

You have the public data of the OAs, the tools of the Multi100 analysts and the choices that they faced. You are analyst no. 6, and the question is how robust that gap is to *justifiable* alternative choices. Work through the five tasks below in order, from a setup check to two marks on the live class chart: an exploratory one from Task 4, and a declared one from Task 5, whose specification you fix in your preregistration before running it.

::: callout-tip
## How the tasks work

Every task is a callout box with instructions, a **TODO** for you to complete, and code chunks that **already run**, so the report renders from the first preview. You edit the prose blanks and, in Tasks 2, 4 and 5, the code. The course site also has a browser version of this exercise, which the facilitator drives on the shared screen and which stands in if your machine fails. This workspace is the full pipeline, worked in an IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.).
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Task 1 – The setup check and the three Rs"}
**First, the setup check.** If this report renders at all, your workspace is working: the packages are installed, the data are in place, and the helpers are loaded. Render it once now, before anything else. If it does not render, run `source("R/check_setup.R")` in the console. It names the packages that you are missing and how to install them, and its last check fits the reference specification of the course, which must come out at −19.97 percentage points.

**Then, before touching data, fix the vocabulary.** Three of the four scenarios below describe one of our three Rs (reproducibility, robustness, replicability), while the fourth describes something else entirely.

**TODO: read the four scenarios and fill in the gaps.**

***Scenario 1:*** A reviewer runs the Stata `.do` file of the OAs on their public data file and gets a coefficient for Hispanic names that differs from the one printed in the paper, because the public file holds the size, poverty and ethnic composition of each community in thirds rather than as the census values. This is an example of \_\_\_\_\_\_, even though the numbers do not match.

***Scenario 2:*** An analyst takes the same public file, re-implements the analysis in R instead of Stata, and also counts the five replies that carry no greeting code as replies without a greeting. Is this a case of \_\_\_\_\_\_ or \_\_\_\_\_\_?

***Scenario 3:*** A preregistered team emails 3,050 public housing authorities with four new names and finds no difference in how often the replies greet the sender by name. Their conclusion is that the original finding has failed to \_\_\_\_\_\_.

***Scenario 4:*** Another researcher asks whether the same bias appears when people telephone school districts rather than email housing authorities, codes recorded voice messages instead of written replies, and finds the same pattern. The researcher concludes that the original finding \_\_\_\_\_\_ to another service and another medium.

*(Answers: 1 reproducibility – the activity is reproduction even though the numbers differ, and the difference has a documented cause, the blinded file; 2 a grey area – re-implementing on the same data in different software is still reproduction, but recoding the uncoded replies is an analytic choice, which makes it a test of robustness; 3 replicability – the same question asked of independent new data; 4 generalisability – the odd one out, with a new population, new data and a new measure at once.)*
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Task 2 – The data"}
The **housing-audit data** (`housing_audit.csv`) hold one row per email. They are already loaded as `audit` in the setup chunk. The file is built from the public file of the OAs on Harvard Dataverse (doi:10.7910/DVN/1HOVTU, released under CC0), with plainer column names; `audit_original.csv`, which Task 3 uses, is that public file with its original names.

**TODO:** run the chunks, then read the figure. Which name received the fewest greetings by name? Note it in a comment.

```{r}
#| label: count-emails
# How many emails, and what came back?
audit |>
  summarise(emails    = n(),
            bounced   = sum(is.na(reply)),
            delivered = sum(!is.na(reply)),
            replies   = sum(reply %in% 1),
            coded     = sum(!is.na(named)))
```

You should find **1,014 emails** (the paper reports 1,017, three more than the public file holds), of which **23 bounced** and never reached an official, **991 delivered**, **563 replies**, and **558 replies with a greeting code**. The column `reply` is 1 for a reply, 0 for none and missing for a bounced email. `named` is 1 when a reply greeted the sender by name, 0 when it did not, and missing for every email without a reply and for the five replies that carry no greeting code. `group` is the group that the name was meant to indicate, and `name` the name itself.

```{r}
#| label: by-group
# Replies and greetings by the group of the name
audit |>
  filter(!is.na(reply)) |>
  summarise(delivered   = n(),
            replies     = sum(reply == 1),
            coded       = sum(!is.na(named)),
            greeted     = sum(named %in% 1),
            greeted_pct = round(100 * greeted / coded, 1),
            .by = group)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-names
#| fig-cap: "Replies that greeted the sender by name, by the name that signed the email."
#| fig-height: 3.6
audit |>
  filter(!is.na(named)) |>
  summarise(greeted_pct = 100 * mean(named), .by = c(group, name)) |>
  mutate(name = reorder(name, greeted_pct)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = greeted_pct, y = name, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", greeted_pct)), hjust = -0.15, size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(white = "grey60", black = "#4a78ab", hispanic = "#8b1538"),
                    labels = c(white = "white", black = "Black", hispanic = "Hispanic"),
                    name = "Names meant to indicate") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(x = "Replies that greeted the sender by name (%)", y = NULL)
```

The replies to white names greeted the sender by name in 61.1% of cases, those to Hispanic names in 41.2%: a gap of about 20 points, the size of the published estimate. Black names fall in between, at 56.1%. Every column is described in `data/housing_audit_codebook.md`.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Task 2, continued – The estimand and the graph"}
Before estimating, say *precisely* what you are estimating. An estimand has two parts: a **unit-specific quantity** and a **target population** (Lundberg et al. 2021). State it outside any model.

**TODO – complete the estimand statement:**

> Unit-specific quantity: for each housing authority, the difference between whether it would come back with \[\_\_\_\_\] to an email signed with a Hispanic name and to the same email signed with \[\_\_\_\_\]. Target population: \[\_\_\_\_\].

*(A defensible filling: a reply that greets the sender by name; a white name; the public housing authorities that received an email. The catch is that an authority whose official would not reply to one of the names has no greeting to compare. The comparison can then count every delivered email, a missing reply counting as no greeting, or count the replies only, which compares the authorities that replied to Hispanic names with those that replied to white names. These need not be the same authorities.)*

A causal graph makes that catch visible. `R/dag_starter.R` builds the graph with `make_dag()`, one arrow per line, each written the way it is drawn: `"name -> reply"` is the arrow from the name to the reply. The name can affect whether the official replies, and only a reply can greet the sender by name. Something about the official that nobody recorded (workload, habits of courtesy, attitudes) affects both whether they reply and how they greet, and so does the community of the housing authority. One arrow is switched off with a `#`: the arrow from the name to the greeting, which is the effect on tone that the claim is about.

```{r}
#| label: fig-dag
#| fig-cap: "The starter graph. The official is unobserved; the arrow from the name to the greeting is still switched off."
#| fig-height: 4.5
source("R/dag_starter.R")
plot_dag(dag)
```

Two questions can be put to the graph. The first is what has to be adjusted for when the comparison counts every delivered email. The second is which paths from the name to the greeting are open once the comparison is made among replies only, which is what `Z = "reply"` asks: it conditions on the reply.

```{r}
#| label: adjustment-set
adjustmentSets(dag)
```

```{r}
#| label: paths-replies
paths(dag)
paths(dag, Z = "reply")
```

`adjustmentSets()` returns `{}`, the empty set: nothing has to be adjusted for, because nothing points into the name. The names were assigned at random, so no common cause of the name and the greeting can exist. Conditioning on the reply changes the picture. The path through the reply closes, but two paths open, one through the community and one through the official, because the reply is a common effect of the name and of each of them (a collider), and comparing replies only conditions on it. This is the problem of conditioning on a consequence of the treatment, which Coppock (2019) sets out for audit experiments.

**TODO:** open `R/dag_starter.R`, take the `#` off the arrow `"name -> greeting"`, save, and run the three chunks above again (or render). Then answer three questions in a sentence each:

1.  Why does `adjustmentSets()` still return `{}`? *(Nothing points into the name, whatever arrows leave it: randomisation.)*
2.  With the arrow switched on, which paths does `paths(dag, Z = c("reply", "community"))` leave open, and what does that mean for a gap among replies? *(The direct path and the path through the official. A gap among replies mixes the effect of the name on tone with differences between the officials who reply to each name, and adjusting for the community cannot remove the second, because the official is unobserved.)*
3.  Which emails keep the comparison randomised, and what does it then estimate? *(Every delivered email, a missing reply counting as no greeting. It estimates the effect of the name on receiving a greeting by name at all, which mixes the decision to reply with the tone of the reply.)*

```{r}
#| label: paths-adjusted
paths(dag, Z = c("reply", "community"))
```

The difference between these two comparisons is the decision on which emails are counted, the second argument of `try_spec()` in Task 4, and whatever you conclude here becomes field 4 of the preregistration that you write in Task 5.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Task 3 – The reproduction"}
This is the **reproducibility** check. Analyst 8PTRZ compared Hispanic names with all other names among the 558 replies that carry a greeting code, with a chi-square test of the 2 × 2 table. Multi100 recorded $\chi^2$ = 14.265. Reproduce it from the public file of the OAs, `audit_original.csv`, which keeps their column names: `ProperName` is the greeting by name and `TreatmentGroup` the name group and sex (`"Hispanic male"`, `"white female"` and so on).

```{r}
#| label: reproduce-8ptrz
original <- read_csv("data/audit_original.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

coded_replies <- original |>
  filter(!is.na(ProperName)) |>
  mutate(hispanic_name = grepl("^Hispanic", TreatmentGroup))

nrow(coded_replies)

tab_8ptrz <- xtabs(~ hispanic_name + ProperName, data = coded_replies)
tab_8ptrz

chisq.test(tab_8ptrz)
```

The test gives **X-squared = 14.265** on 1 df, the value on record for analyst 8PTRZ, reproduced from the public data. Type your $\chi^2$ into the chat, hold it, and send it on the facilitator's word.

Now find out why it is 14.265. For a 2 × 2 table, `chisq.test()` applies the continuity correction of Yates unless it is told otherwise: it shrinks each gap between an observed and an expected count by 0.5 before squaring, a remedy designed for small tables. The analyst did not choose it; the default of the function did.

```{r}
#| label: reproduce-uncorrected
chisq.test(tab_8ptrz, correct = FALSE)
```

Without the correction the statistic is 14.95. Neither number changes the conclusion, but only one of them matches the record, and the description "a chi-square test" fits both. A reproduction needs the code, or at least every default that the code relied on.

*Optional extension.* Analyst UYV3F compared Hispanic with white names only, among their 362 coded replies, with a logistic regression and no covariates. Multi100 recorded z = −3.771:

```{r}
#| label: reproduce-uyv3f
m_uyv3f <- glm(ProperName ~ hispanic_name, family = binomial(),
               data = filter(coded_replies, !grepl("^black", TreatmentGroup)))
nobs(m_uyv3f)
coef(summary(m_uyv3f))
```

The same steps are in `prep/reproduce_8PTRZ.R` as a script. The scripts that the analysts submitted are on the OSF, in the Multi100 component of the paper (osf.io/38rsh); that of 8PTRZ is at osf.io/j8wvh.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Reproduction and the five analysts"}
You reproduced the recorded value exactly, and so did everyone else in the class, because everyone ran the same code on the same file. That is why reproducibility is the cheapest of the three Rs to establish.

The five Multi100 analysts each wrote their own code for this claim. Three concluded that the results were evidence for the claim and two that they were evidence neither for nor against it, although the four statistics that Multi100 recorded all come from gaps in the same direction. Part of the difference lies in the questions that each analyst chose to answer (which names to compare, which emails to count), and part in what each analyst took to count as evidence: one of the two who answered 'neither' found the gap but judged it substantially smaller than the published one. The [case study](https://codemoreh.github.io/applied-replication-housing/cases/housing/index.html) on the course site sets out what each analyst chose.

In Task 2 you named the quantity that you are after and drew the graph that shows what each comparison conditions on. In Task 4 you will find out how far the answer moves when the choices change.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Task 4 – The menu"}
This task is **exploratory**. Try several specifications, look at what each one does, and get a feel for which choices move the estimate and which barely touch it. The specification that you submit with `submit_exploration()` at the end of this task appears on the class chart as an open circle, labelled exploratory. The declared one, a filled circle, is fixed later, in the preregistration block of Task 5, before it is run. Both carry the tag that `submit_exploration()` prints, such as `amber-otter-42`, which is kept in the file `.class-tag` of this workspace and lets you find your own marks on the chart. To choose your own, write `submit_exploration(nickname = "...")` with a nickname rather than your name, because the chart is public.

`try_spec()` takes one argument per decision of the specification menu. Every argument defaults to the reference specification, the raw gap of the paper (Hispanic against white names, among the replies, the five uncoded replies left out, a difference in proportions without covariates), so changing one thing means changing one argument. Every call is a live fit on your machine. The first five arguments are the decisions on which the curve of the claim keeps more than one option:

- `comparison` – white names (`"white"`), or white and Black names together (`"nonhispanic"`);
- `population` – the replies only (`"replies"`), or every delivered email with no reply counted as no greeting (`"all"`);
- `uncoded` – the five replies without a greeting code left out (`"drop"`) or counted as no greeting (`"not_named"`);
- `model` – a linear probability model, whose coefficient is the difference in proportions (`"lpm"`), or the logistic regression of the paper, reported as an average marginal effect (`"logit"`);
- `adjust` – no covariates (`"none"`), the hard-to-find address (`"email"`), that and the size and poverty of the community (`"place"`), or those and its ethnic composition (`"place_ethnic"`), all in the thirds of the public file.

The printout gives the shares greeted by name in the two groups, the difference in percentage points with its 95% interval, the test of the model (a *t* with HC2 standard errors for the linear model, the *z* of the logit coefficient for the logit), the number of emails analysed, the partial *r* by the conversion rule of Multi100, the class of the result, and its place among the 64 specifications on the curve.

**TODO:** run the six calls below and the refused one after them, then write your own. Three or four of your own is plenty.
:::

```{r}
#| label: try-reference
try_spec()                               # the reference specification itself
```

```{r}
#| label: try-one-at-a-time
try_spec(comparison = "nonhispanic")     # Hispanic names against white and Black names together
try_spec(population = "all")             # every delivered email, no reply counted as no greeting
try_spec(uncoded    = "not_named")       # the five uncoded replies counted as no greeting
try_spec(model      = "logit")           # the model of the paper, as an average marginal effect
try_spec(adjust     = "place_ethnic")    # the covariates of the original model, in thirds
```

The first two calls change the question that is being asked of the data, the third changes how the outcome is measured, and the last two change only how the same question is estimated. The menu holds more options than the curve, which keeps only the options that answer this claim in a justifiable way. Every other option is still an argument of `try_spec()`, and trying one is part of the exercise: the helper refuses it, gives the reason why it is not on the curve, and names the page of the course site that teaches it. The next chunk stops with that reason, and the report still renders because the chunk is marked `error: true`. Edit it to try others, such as `outcome = "reply"`, `names = "male"`, `comparison = "black"`, `adjust = "acs_continuous"` or `inference = "one_tailed"`:

```{r}
#| label: try-off-curve
#| error: true
try_spec(model = "three_group")          # all three groups in one model: refused, with the reason why
```

Everything you try is logged. Print the log to view the small multiverse that you have just built. Only the decisions that you varied are shown, which keeps the comparison readable:

```{r}
#| label: my-experiments
my_experiments()
```

When you have tried three or four, decide which one you would defend if you had to, run it once more so that it is the most recent, and submit it. It appears on the live class chart as an **exploratory** result:

```{r}
#| label: submit-exploration
#| eval: false
submit_exploration()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Exploratory and declared"}
You chose this specification after finding out what several of them do, so it lacks the guarantee that a choice fixed in a preregistration before it is run carries: it might have been chosen *because* of its result, and neither you nor anyone else can now rule that out.

Almost no published paper reports which of its analyses were explored and which were planned. The class chart does, because everyone submits twice: once here, and once in Task 5 after preregistering a specification, so that the two sets of marks can be read against each other.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Task 5 – The preregistration"}
A preregistration fixes your specification **before** you know its result, which stops you from quietly picking the one that happens to give the answer you wanted. In a real study it is filed, with a date stamp, in a public registry such as the OSF. In this report the preregistration is the block below, and the code enforces it: the R session keeps the choices that you set in that block, and `run_spec()` and `report_result()` read them from there.

Make one choice on each decision of the menu, complete the dotted lines, then run the block. The five decisions at Level 1 fix the question that you are asking, the two at Level 2 fix how the outcome is measured, and the four at Level 3 fix how it is estimated. The curve of 64 specifications keeps two or more options on five of these decisions and a single option on the other six. An option that is not on the curve stops `prereg()` with the reason why, as it stops `try_spec()`.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="How this block maps to a real preregistration"}
*A real preregistration, shortened. Each numbered comment maps to a question in the OSF "Preregistration Template from AsPredicted.org" (the eight-question short form). Because you are reanalysing data that already exist, field 2 also stands in for the prior-knowledge section of the secondary-data template (van den Akker et al. 2021) – the part that AsPredicted leaves out.*
:::

```{r}
#| label: prereg
# ============================================================================
# MY PREREGISTRATION – one specification, declared before seeing its result
# ============================================================================
# 1. The claim I am testing: .................................................
# 2. The data + what I already know: housing_audit.csv (1,014 emails, public,
#    CC0); I know that the reference specification gives -19.97 points, and
#    what my exploration in Task 4 showed.
# 3. My one specification – one choice on each decision. An option that is
#    not on the curve of 64 stops prereg() with the reason why.

# Level 1 – Estimands (each of these changes what is being estimated)
my_outcome    <- "named"     # named   (greeted by name, the outcome of the claim)
my_comparison <- "white"     # white | nonhispanic   (white names, or white and Black names)
my_population <- "replies"   # replies | all   (replies only, or every delivered email)
my_names      <- "both"      # both   (male and female names pooled)
my_officials  <- "any"       # any    (replies from every official)

# Level 2 – Measurement (the same question, put to the data differently)
my_uncoded    <- "drop"      # drop | not_named   (the five replies without a greeting code)
my_bounced    <- "exclude"   # exclude   (the 23 emails that never arrived)

# Level 3 – Estimation (the same question and measures, another fit)
my_model      <- "lpm"       # lpm | logit   (difference in proportions, or logistic regression)
my_adjust     <- "none"      # none | email | place | place_ethnic
my_inference  <- "model"     # model   (HC2 t test, or the z test of the logit)
my_scale      <- "pp"        # pp   (percentage points)

# 4. Why this specification answers the claim, in one sentence grounded in
#    the causal graph of Task 2: .............................................
# 5. Supported if the estimate is below zero with p < .05 under the test of
#    the model; undermined if it is not significant or above zero. I will
#    report what I get.

my_spec <- prereg()   # checks every choice, prints your preregistration and keeps it
```

The block above, rendered into this report, is your preregistration.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

::: {.callout-note title="Task 5, continued – Fit, report and place"}
This is the **robustness** check, and it is the part that your classmates cannot copy from you. Together, the class samples the multiverse of defensible analyses. Your specification is fixed in the preregistration block above. `run_spec()` fits it for real and prints the same lines as `try_spec()`; it refuses to run if the block has changed since `prereg()` read it.
:::

```{r}
#| label: run-spec
run_spec(my_spec)
```

Read the output like an analyst. The difference is in percentage points, and a value below zero means that replies to Hispanic names greeted the sender by name less often, the direction of the claim. Whether it is significant is decided by the test of the model, and the line headed `Class:` says which of the four cases your result falls in. The last line places it among the 64 specifications of the curve.

Now submit it to the class chart. There is nothing to fill in and nothing to transcribe: `report_result()` refits your preregistered specification, builds the spec label, and prints your submission line and a pre-filled form link. Open it and press **Send**. Your mark appears on the live [Multiverse](https://codemoreh.github.io/applied-replication-housing/cases/housing/multiverse.html) chart within seconds, this time as a filled circle labelled **declared**, with the same tag as your exploratory result.

```{r}
#| label: report
report_result()
```

If the form will not open on your machine, read the printed numbers to the facilitator and your mark will still be added.

Finally, place your result on the curve of the claim: the 64 specifications that the menu keeps, ranked from the most negative estimate, with yours ringed.

```{r}
#| label: fig-curve
#| fig-cap: "The curve of 64 specifications, coloured by the emails counted; your declared specification is ringed."
spec_curve <- read_csv("data/spec_curve.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  arrange(b_pp) |>
  mutate(rank = row_number(),
         mine = comparison == my_comparison & population == my_population &
           uncoded == my_uncoded & model == my_model & adjust == my_adjust)

ggplot(spec_curve, aes(x = rank, y = b_pp)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = population), size = 2) +
  geom_point(data = filter(spec_curve, mine), shape = 21, size = 5, stroke = 1.2,
             colour = "#8b1538") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(replies = "#0e3b6a", all = "#2b8585"),
                      breaks = c("replies", "all"),
                      labels = c(replies = "replies only", all = "all delivered emails"),
                      name = "Emails counted") +
  labs(x = "The 64 specifications, from the most negative estimate",
       y = "Hispanic minus comparison names (points)")
```

All 64 estimates lie below zero, from −20.0 to −12.1 points, and every one of them is significant at 5% under the test of its model. The two clusters are the two answers to the decision on which emails are counted: counting every delivered email moves the estimate about 5 points towards zero, and no other decision moves it by more than about 2.7 points. Within these data the claim holds under every choice on the menu, and only its size moves.

**A second declared specification?** Edit the preregistration block, rerun it, then rerun `run_spec(my_spec)`. The mechanics allow it, and the label does not change, so be clear with yourself about what the second one is. Your first preregistration was made without knowing its result. Anything after it was not, which puts it back in the same category as Task 4, and you should say so when you report it.

::: {.callout-note title="Going further (optional)"}
Each of these runs in this workspace if you have time to spare.

- **Sweep a whole decision.** `purrr::walk(c("none", "email", "place", "place_ethnic"), \(a) try_spec(adjust = a))` fits the four adjustment sets in one go, and `my_experiments()` then prints them side by side. The same call works for any decision on which the curve keeps more than one option.

- **The five analysts on the curve.** `data/reference_marks.csv` places the published result, by its published change in predicted probability, and the five Multi100 analyses, each by a course refit on the public data, in percentage points (`b_pp`); keep the rows with `on_chart` TRUE other than `SCORE`, which places the replication on new data. Add them to the figure above as horizontal lines with `geom_hline()`, and find where the analysis of 25N5D, the only one to count every delivered email, falls among the 64.

- **A second test.** Every row of `data/spec_curve.csv` also carries `p_ri`, the p-value of a randomisation test that reshuffles the names among the analysed emails 1,999 times. Compare it with `p`, the test of the model. Because the names were assigned at random, the reshuffling reproduces the design of the experiment itself.

- **New data.** The SCORE replication emailed 3,050 public housing authorities in a preregistered design, with four new male names, two meant to indicate Hispanic and two white senders, and found no difference in greetings by name: z = 0.66, p = 0.511 on a random draw of 738 replies. A claim can hold under every analytic choice on one sample and still fail on new data. The report and the preregistration of the replication are on the OSF, at <https://osf.io/2ug8x/>.
:::
